title: Enough
excerpt: Agur prayed for just enough: keep me honest and give me my daily bread. Proverbs on contentment, and the One who became poor for us.

blocks.text: Buried near the end of Proverbs is a man almost nobody talks about.

His name is Agur. We don't know where he lived, what he did, or how old he was. The Bible gives us a single chapter of his sayings, and tucked inside it is one short prayer. It might be the most unusual prayer in Scripture, because of what he leaves out.

verses: Two things I ask of you, LORD; do not refuse me before I die: Keep falsehood and lies far from me; give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me only my daily bread.

blocks.text: Read that again slowly. He is asking God for two things before he dies, and he can ask for *anything.* And what he asks for is: keep me honest, and give me just enough.
Not more. Not a bigger house, a better position, a safer cushion. *Just enough.*
When was the last time you prayed that?
The Prayer Nobody Prays

Most of us, if we're honest, pray in the other direction. We pray for provision, which is fine, and Jesus told us to. But somewhere underneath, we often mean *more.* More income. More security. More room in the budget, more margin, a little bit more than we have now, because then we'd finally relax.

The trouble is that "more" has no finish line. Reach it, and a new one appears. Agur seems to know this. A few verses later, he describes a pair of leech's daughters, hungry creatures whose only word is "Give! Give!" (30:15). And then he lists four things that never get filled up, four things that never say, "Enough!" (30:15–16). The grave. The barren womb. Thirsty land. Fire. And somewhere nearby, in another proverb, the human eye: "Death and Destruction are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes" (27:20).
That's how Proverbs describes our wanting. Like fire, it doesn't stop when it's fed. It only grows.
So the first thing Agur's prayer does is quietly cut against our whole way of living. He's saying: *I've decided there's such a thing as enough, and I'd like to ask God to help me find it.*
Why Not Riches?
Here's where Agur surprises us even more. It's easy to see why he doesn't want poverty. But why would a man of faith ask *not* to be rich? Isn't wealth a blessing?
He explains himself, and the reasoning is remarkably honest:

verses: Otherwise, I may have too much and disown you and say, 'Who is the LORD?' Or I may become poor and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God.

blocks.text: He fears both extremes, and for the same reason. Not because money is evil, but because of what each side does to a person's heart.

Having too much, he says, might make me forget God. When everything is provided for, when the accounts are full and the future feels safe, it's easy to stop praying. We stop needing Him, and without noticing, we start saying with our lives, *Who is the LORD?* Few people decide to leave God. Plenty simply drift when they stop needing Him.
And having too little might make me desperate enough to compromise. Poverty isn't a moral failing, and Agur doesn't treat it as one. He's being realistic about how pressure bends people.
What's striking is that he knows himself. He doesn't assume he'd handle wealth well. Most of us pray for more without ever asking whether we could carry it. Agur asked the harder question first.
Money Has Wings

Elsewhere, Proverbs puts it plainly. "Do not wear yourself out to get rich; do not trust your own cleverness. Cast but a glance at riches, and they are gone, for they surely sprout wings and fly off to the sky like an eagle" (23:4–5).

That image sticks with me. You glance at it, and it's gone. Anyone who has watched savings vanish to a medical bill, a layoff, or a market drop knows this isn't theoretical. The things we most trust to hold us up are the most fragile things we own. "Those who trust in their riches will fall," the book says, "but the righteous will thrive like a green leaf" (11:28).

And it isn't only about money leaving. It's about what the chase takes from us while it's here. "Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great wealth with turmoil" (15:16). "Better a dry crust with peace and quiet than a house full of feasting, with strife" (17:1). Proverbs keeps returning to the same strange math: a small amount with peace beats a large amount with anxiety. Anyone who has lived on both sides of that equation knows it's true.
A Lesson from the Desert
None of this was new for God's people. They had learned it the hard way, in the wilderness, with a daily lesson in bread.

After the exodus, with no food and nowhere to buy any, God sent manna from heaven, a fresh supply every morning. There was one rule: gather what you need for today. Some people, understandably nervous, tried to store extra overnight. By morning it had spoiled and was full of worms (Exodus 16:19–20).

God wasn't being harsh. He was teaching them to trust Him daily, to wake up depending on Him. Not hoarding, not anxious, just receiving. It's exactly what Agur means by "my daily bread," and it's why Jesus taught His disciples to pray, "Give us today our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). Not a year's supply. Today's.

That can feel uncomfortable, especially if you're someone who likes to plan ahead. And planning is good. Proverbs praises the ant that stores up in summer. But there's a line between wise planning and a heart that can't rest unless it has a buffer of its own making. The first is stewardship. The second is a quiet way of saying *I'm not sure God will be there.*
If "Enough" Feels Out of Reach

I want to say something to the reader who finished that last section feeling the opposite of content. Maybe you're counting every dollar. Maybe "enough" isn't a spiritual question for you right now, it's a rent question, a grocery question, a how-do-I-get-through-this-month question.

If that's you, hear this clearly: this passage isn't a lecture. Agur doesn't treat need as shameful, and neither does the God he's praying to. Jesus said, "Your heavenly Father knows that you need them" (Matthew 6:32). He sees the specifics. And Agur's prayer is, at its root, a prayer of dependence, one you can pray right where you are. *Give me today's bread.* Not as a technique, but as an honest request to a Father who has promised to hear it.
The One Who Gave Up Everything
This is where the whole thing turns from advice into good news.

We're tempted to chase "more" because we believe, deep down, that something is missing. That if we just had enough money, enough safety, enough success, we'd finally feel secure. But the gospel tells a different story about who we are. We aren't people who lack. We're people who have been given everything.

"For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). The One who owned everything gave it all up, not to teach us a lesson about budgeting, but to make us heirs of the very thing money could never buy. Peace with God. A place at His table. A future that can't spoil.

And that's why Hebrews can say something that would sound ridiculous anywhere else: "Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, because God has said, 'Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you'" (13:5). Notice the reason. Not "be content because you have enough stuff." Be content because *you have Him.* Contentment isn't a feeling we manufacture. It's what grows when we realize the One who gave Himself for us isn't going anywhere.

So, what would "enough" look like for you? Not a number in a bank account, but a place where you could honestly say, *God has provided. I can rest.* Maybe it's closer than you think. Maybe it already is.

items: If you're honest, what is your "just a little more"? More income, more security, a bigger house, a better title. What do you believe it would finally give you, and has anything you've reached so far actually delivered that?

Which side of Agur's fear is more true of you right now: forgetting God because you feel provided for, or being tempted to compromise because you feel the pressure? What does that tell you about where you most need to depend on Him?

What would it look like to practice "daily bread" this week? Is there an area where you've been trying to control the future, and what would it mean to hand today's need to God and trust Him with tomorrow?

blocks.text: Lord, I confess how often I pray for more without asking whether I could handle it. Keep falsehood far from me. Teach me what enough looks like, and give me my daily bread. Free me from the quiet fear that makes me hold too tightly, and from the pride that forgets You when things are good. Thank You that in Christ I already have what matters most. Help me rest in that, and be generous with what You've given. Amen.
